look_here_first: Introduced in many Texas floras. Look for an annual with decumbent or creeping rooted stems and a LOOSE spreading/ascending set of slender flowering racemes (unlike dense blunt-headed U. fusca). Measure a tiny ~1.5–2.5 mm ovoid spikelet and look for the almost missing basal glume; a seedhead photo alone does not show rooted basal nodes.

best_field_traits: Usually creeping or ascending warm-season annual, frequently in disturbed moist sites.
Racemes relatively slender with spaced tiny spikelets rather than dense plump cylindrical clusters.
Spikelets much smaller (~1.5–2.5 mm) than U. texana; lower glume almost minute, ~15–25% of length.
Upper glume and sterile lemma occupy most of spikelet; tough fertile lemma and palea transversely wrinkled.
Creeping basal shoots may root at nodes; must be seen/photographed to assert.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Whole plant with any actual stem node rooting
Panicle in profile showing loose branch spacing
Individual tiny mature spikelet with calibrated scale
Macro tiny clasping lower glume versus U. texana
True collar ligule and sheath hair bases
crew_field_check: START WITH THREE SIGNALGRASS HEADS: U. fusca has tight rather chunky spikelet clusters; U. reptans forms a much more delicate spreading narrow-branched head; U. texana has larger (~4.5–6 mm) spikelets along alternate ascending branches. These silhouettes HELP, but reliable separation depends on measuring mature spikelets and the proportion of the LOWER GLUME.
Measure actual mature spikelet(s) with a millimeter ruler.
Inspect lemma/glume or true ligule ONLY where detailed pixels or a collected macro are actually available.
Record uncertain grass to genus, don't force the species from one photo.

comparisons.key_distinctions: U. fusca tends to have densely clustered blunt plump spikelets ~2.4–3 mm. U. texana has comparatively large 4.5–6 mm elongated spikelets and looser ascending branches on a stouter habit. Compare with Digitaria ciliaris if fingerlike racemes dominate: paired spikelets and membranous ligule are relevant. The 'creeping' name alone does not identify a sterile individual.
